vignette:
He is seventy-four now, a widower who still wakes before dawn as if someone has handed him a flight schedule. For most of his adult life, he is known as steady under pressure. He flies combat missions when he is young and learns to trust procedure, instruments, and the part of himself that can go cold in danger. Even after retirement, he keeps that same discipline. He folds his clothes neatly over a chair, polishes old aviator sunglasses he no longer wears, and checks the locks on the doors each night in the same order. People who meet him casually take him for a man who has seen difficult things and managed them well.

He says the trouble that brings him in does not begin in the air or overseas. It begins much later, after his wife dies. The house becomes unbearably quiet. He misses the ordinary companionship of another person moving through the kitchen, asking if he wants coffee, leaving a book open on the arm of the sofa. A few years into widowhood, he meets a woman at a community event for veterans and seniors. At first she seems lively and attentive. She tells him she admires men with discipline, men who have served. He feels rusty and a little embarrassed by how much her interest means to him.

The relationship moves quickly. She begins spending nights at his home, then most of the week. Early on, he notices flashes of temper that he explains away. She mocks the way he keeps things organized. She accuses him of being emotionally distant when he wants an evening to himself. If he does not answer a call right away, she leaves a string of messages that swing from pleading to furious. He tells himself he has handled worse. He is a trained pilot, not some helpless old man. He thinks if he stays calm, the weather will pass.

Instead, her anger becomes physical. The first time, they are in the kitchen. She is drinking, upset that he has declined to lend money to her son. He turns away to end the argument, and she strikes him across the face with surprising force. He remembers not pain at first but disorientation, the surreal pause afterward, as if his mind cannot match what has happened to the room he is standing in. She cries almost immediately, says she is under terrible stress, says he has no idea how hard life has been for her. He hears himself comforting her.

After that, he begins living in anticipation. He studies the set of her jaw, the speed of her footsteps in the hallway, the sound of cupboards closing. He removes objects from the kitchen counters because he starts imagining what could be thrown. He avoids certain topics, then most topics. On bad nights she shoves him in the chest, scratches his forearms, once hits him with a cordless phone hard enough to leave a bruise near his temple. He does not tell friends. The shame feels bigger than the injuries. He thinks no one will believe a former combat pilot is being beaten by his partner in his own home. He imagines the look on another veteran’s face if he were to say it out loud.

What disturbs him most is how small his world becomes. He starts jumping at sudden movement. When she raises her voice, his heart pounds so hard he feels it in his throat. Sometimes, in the middle of an argument, everything narrows and sharpens: the clink of ice in her glass, the pattern in the wallpaper, the route to the back door. At other times he goes strangely blank, as if he is watching from high above and cannot get his body to move. He hates that feeling. It reminds him of nothing from combat, he says, because in combat he knew who the enemy was and what he was supposed to do.

The relationship ends after she pushes him from behind during an argument on the back steps. He falls hard, bruising his hip and wrist. He lies there for a moment stunned, looking at the winter grass and feeling older than he has ever felt. A neighbor hears shouting and comes outside. That witness, he says, is what finally breaks the spell. She leaves that night.

He expects relief, but the danger does not seem to leave with her. Months later he still scans parking lots before getting out of the car. He keeps the television on low for company yet startles when commercials get too loud. If a woman in a store speaks sharply to someone nearby, his chest tightens and his hands go cold. He no longer invites people over because he cannot bear the thought of explaining the broken picture frame he never replaced or the stain on the wall in the hallway. He sleeps in short stretches and wakes alert, listening. Some mornings he sits at the edge of the bed already exhausted.

He is troubled by memories that intrude without warning: the crack of the phone against his head, her footsteps coming down the hall, the instant before he hits the ground outside. He tries to push them away, but that only seems to make them return more vividly. He has begun avoiding the community center where they met. He rarely sees old friends from his flying days. He tells himself he prefers solitude, but in session he admits the loneliness has curdled into something harsher. He feels embarrassed, watchful, easily angered, and not at all like the man he spent a lifetime becoming.
